questions.question: In the Hungarian algorithm for an $n\times n$ assignment cost matrix, the zeros of the current reduced matrix are covered with as few row and column lines as possible. When can a complete assignment be read off from the zeros?
options: When every row contains at least one zero.
When the matrix contains at least $n$ zeros.
When this minimum cover needs $n$ lines.
When fewer than $n$ lines cover all zeros.

questions.question: During the Hungarian algorithm on a $5\times5$ assignment cost matrix, the zeros of the current reduced matrix can be covered by 4 row or column lines, and no cover with fewer lines exists. How many zeros can be chosen with no two in the same row or column?
options: Exactly 4, the size of the minimum cover
Exactly 5, since the matrix has 5 rows
Exactly 1, the shortfall from 5 to 4
At most 4, since the lines only give an upper bound

questions.question: The Hungarian algorithm subtracts the smallest entry of each row from that row of an $n\times n$ assignment cost matrix, and then does the same for each column. Why does this not change which complete assignments are optimal?
options: The subtraction keeps every entry nonnegative, which preserves the ranking.
Each row minimum is part of the optimal assignment, so it is removed anyway.
All entries fall by the same constant, so all entry comparisons are kept.
Each assignment uses every row and column once, so all totals fall equally.

questions.question: After the row, column and adjustment steps of the Hungarian algorithm, an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix contains $n$ zeros with no two in the same row or column. Why is the assignment using these zeros optimal for the original costs?
options: Each chosen zero marks the cheapest original cost in its own row.
No reduced entry is negative, so no assignment has a reduced total below 0.
Using only zero entries gives an original total cost of 0.
Each adjustment lowered the optimal cost until it could not fall further.

questions.question: In the Hungarian algorithm for a $3\times3$ assignment cost matrix, each row minimum has been subtracted from its row, and column 2 of the result contains no zero. What follows?
options: Task 2 can be dropped, since a column without a zero is never used.
No complete zero assignment exists yet, so column 2's minimum is subtracted.
The row minima must be subtracted again until column 2 has a zero.
Column 2 is covered by a line first, since covering precedes the column step.

questions.question: For the assignment cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}7&3&6\\5&4&9\\8&6&7\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks and entry $(i,j)$ is the cost of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), the Hungarian algorithm first subtracts each row minimum. Which amounts are then subtracted from columns 1, 2 and 3?
options: 5, 3 and 6
0, 0 and 0
4, 0 and 3
1, 0 and 1

questions.question: In the Hungarian algorithm, the reduced matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&8&3\\1&0&0\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix}$ has all its zeros covered by the minimum cover of row 2 and column 1. Which matrix results from one adjustment step?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&7&2\\2&0&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&7&2\\1&0&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&7&2\\2&1&1\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&7&2\\0&0&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: For the assignment cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}4&2&9\\2&2&1\\5&2&7\end{pmatrix}$ (rows are agents, columns are tasks and entry $(i,j)$ is the cost of giving task $j$ to agent $i$), the Hungarian algorithm (row step, column step, one adjustment) ends with independent zeros at positions $(1,1)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$. What is the minimum total cost?
In the Hungarian algorithm, which set of lines is a minimum cover of all zeros of the reduced matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0&2\\4&1&0\\7&5&0\end{pmatrix}$?
options: Row 1 and column 3
Columns 1 and 3
Rows 1, 2 and 3
Rows 1 and 2

questions.question: The final reduced matrix of a Hungarian algorithm run is $\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\7&5&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$, with rows as agents and columns as tasks. Which positions (row, column) form the complete zero assignment?

In a Hungarian adjustment step, $k$ is subtracted from every uncovered entry and added to every entry covered by two lines. Why is $k$ taken to be the smallest uncovered entry rather than any uncovered entry?
options: Any uncovered entry works; the smallest just keeps numbers small.
It guarantees that the next minimum cover has exactly one more line.
It creates a new zero and keeps every entry nonnegative.
It is the amount later added to the zero assignment's cost.

questions.question: A student applies the Hungarian algorithm to a square assignment cost matrix but subtracts the column minima first and the row minima afterwards, then continues as usual. What is the effect of this change of order?
options: It is invalid, since column minima are defined only after the row step.
It remains valid; the reduced matrix may differ, but not the optimum.
It is valid only if all row minima lie in different columns.
It stays valid but always needs one extra adjustment step.

questions.question: In the Hungarian algorithm, all zeros of a reduced matrix are covered by a minimum set of lines, and an adjustment step is made with smallest uncovered entry $k>0$. Which zeros of the matrix can stop being zero?
options: Zeros covered by exactly one of the lines
Uncovered zeros, since $k$ is subtracted there
No zeros, since an adjustment only adds new ones
Zeros where a covering row meets a covering column

questions.question: A $3\times3$ profit matrix $\begin{pmatrix}7&5&8\\6&4&3\\9&6&5\end{pmatrix}$ gives the profit of assigning agent $i$ (row) to task $j$ (column), and total profit is to be made as large as possible. Each profit $p_{ij}$ is replaced by the cost $10-p_{ij}$, and the Hungarian algorithm gives minimum total cost 9. What is the maximum total profit?

Apply the Hungarian algorithm to the assignment cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&2&9\\3&5&4\\4&5&8\end{pmatrix}$, where rows are agents, columns are tasks and entry $(i,j)$ is the cost of giving task $j$ to agent $i$. What is the minimum total cost?

For a $3\times3$ assignment cost matrix, the row minima are 4, 5 and 4; after subtracting them, the column minima are 0, 2 and 0. A planner proposes a complete assignment whose total original cost is 15. What can be concluded?
options: Nothing yet; optimality needs a minimum cover with 3 lines first.
It is optimal, since every complete assignment costs at least 15.
Some assignment may cost 13, the sum of the row minima.
It is optimal only if it uses the cheapest entry of each row.

questions.question: The Hungarian algorithm for an $n\times n$ matrix requires the zeros to be covered with the minimum possible number of row and column lines. Why would counting the lines of an arbitrary cover not tell whether $n$ independent zeros exist?
options: The $n$ row lines always cover every zero, so $n$ lines prove nothing.
A non-minimum cover may miss zeros, so some zeros stay unused.
Only a minimum cover makes the smallest uncovered entry positive.
Extra lines change the reduced costs and hence the optimal assignment.

questions.question: In the Hungarian algorithm on an $n\times n$ reduced matrix, a minimum cover uses $L<n$ lines and $k$ is the smallest uncovered entry. How does one adjustment step change the reduced total of each complete assignment?
options: Each total falls by $k$ times its number of uncovered entries.
No total changes, because only nonzero entries are altered.
Every total falls by $k(n-L)$, so the ranking is kept.
Every total falls by $k$, because exactly one new zero appears.

questions.question: A reduced $4\times4$ assignment matrix in the Hungarian algorithm is $\begin{pmatrix}0&0&3&2\\0&4&1&5\\0&2&6&1\\4&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$; every row and every column contains a zero. What is the minimum number of lines covering all zeros, and what is the next step?
options: 4 lines; a complete zero assignment can be chosen now.
2 lines, column 1 and row 4; an adjustment is needed.
3 lines; assign three zeros and give the last agent any free task.
3 lines; an adjustment step is needed first.

questions.question: Three agents must each receive exactly one of three tasks. Rows of $\begin{pmatrix}6&1&5\\4&1&6\\6&7&9\end{pmatrix}$ are agents, columns are tasks, and entry $(i,j)$ is the cost of agent $i$ doing task $j$. What is the smallest possible total cost of a complete assignment, as found by the Hungarian algorithm?
